transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Hello Ms. Patel, I am Dr. Miller. I am one of the residents working on the team taking care of you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Hi. Is the lead doctor coming in?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: He is currently in another patient's room, but I wanted to come in and talk with you as soon as possible about your imaging results from yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Which imaging? The CT scan?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes, that one. There was an issue with how the results were communicated.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What does that mean?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Well, the preliminary report didn't include everything, so there was a bit of a delay in getting the treatment started.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A delay? I've been lying here for nearly a day. What exactly was delayed?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We had some confusion with the radiology report. It took some time for the attending physician to review the images and see the pulmonary embolism.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Wait. You're saying there was a blood clot in my lung and you guys didn't see it?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was visible on the scan, but it wasn't in the first report we received.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So for how long was that just sitting there?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: About eighteen hours.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Eighteen hours. I was literally telling the nurse I felt short of breath and she told me it was just anxiety.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can hear how frustrating that is. It sounds incredibly frightening to feel like your symptoms are being dismissed while something serious is happening inside your body.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It's not just frustrating. It's typical. This is exactly why I don't trust this process. You people just glance at a screen and assume you know everything.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You've had experiences in the past where you felt let down by the medical system, and now it feels like we are just proving you right. That is a heavy thing to carry.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Exactly. So who messed up? Was it the person reading the scan or the person ordering it?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was a systemic failure in the reporting process. The preliminary read didn't catch the embolus, and the final review took longer than it should have.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That is a very corporate way of saying someone failed to do their job. Who is taking responsibility for this?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The process was flawed.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm not talking about a process. I'm talking about a person. Did a doctor miss a clot in my lung for almost a whole day?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The images were there, but the report was incomplete.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You aren't answering me. Did you miss it? Did the radiologist miss it?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: There were gaps in the communication between the departments.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This is unbelievable. You're just dodging. Are you even going to apologize for the fact that I was at risk for another clot or a stroke or whatever because of your gap in communication?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand that you are angry and that you feel unsafe right now. It's completely valid to feel that the trust has been broken here.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Trust was never there to begin with. I want to know exactly what happens now. I'm not signing anything until I see the actual records.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I completely respect that. I'll make sure you have full access to the imaging reports. In terms of the plan, we have started you on the heparin drip, which is the blood thinner.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: For how long?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We will keep you on this drip for the next four days. I will be checking your blood levels every morning at eight a.m. to make sure the dose is safe.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And what happens if another report comes back wrong?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will personally review every single one of your labs and scans with the attending physician before they are entered into your chart for the rest of your stay.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I want that in writing.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can write that down for you right now and put it in your chart. Do you have any other questions about the medication?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I have a lot of questions. Starting with why this is okay.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It isn't okay. I know this has been a distressing experience for you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You're very good at saying you understand, but you still haven't said the words.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see that it's important to you that I acknowledge the failure.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm waiting.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The system failed to alert us in time.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You're doing it again.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Just tell me what the next step is before I change my mind about staying here.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The next step is the blood work at eight tomorrow. Then, we will schedule a follow-up scan for next week to ensure the clot is dissolving. I will be the one to call you with those results directly.

H.justification: The resident never interrupts the patient, remains regulated despite significant pushback, and allows the patient to express anger without rushing.

E.justification: The error (pulmonary embolism) is named, but the resident never checks for patient comprehension of the explanation.

A.justification: The resident never uses direct apology language ('I'm sorry' or 'I apologize') and repeatedly deflects responsibility to 'systemic failure' and 'the process'.

R.justification: The resident names specific emotions ('frustrating', 'frightening', 'angry', 'unsafe') and references the patient's shared history of medical mistrust.

T.justification: The resident provides specific next steps and timelines (heparin for 4 days, blood work at 8am), but does not define a role for the patient in the plan.
